articles.title: FBI questions donors as 2 Dan Sullivans compete in Alaska Senate race
articles.description: ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The FBI on Friday began reaching out to donors of Dan J. Sullivan asking about potential deception, as federal authorities ramped up their investigation over the U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska who shares a name with the Republican incumbent. An Anchorage-based FBI agent visited a boat dealership in Petersburg, a small fishing community accessible only by air or water where the candidate lives. The agent left a business card for Charles Flint, who told The Associated Press he has known Dan J. Sullivan for years as a respected teacher and musician. The FBI visit came after federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over the candidate. The U.S. Department of Justice also pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion. Flint contributed $500 over the summer to what he considered a long-shot campaign, saying he knew Dan J. Sullivan would have expenses and respected him for “throwing his hat in the ring.” Flint said the FBI agent asked his son, who works at the dealership, whether Flint felt he had been “misled” about which candidate he was supporting. “I don’t feel like I’ve been misled at all,” Flint, who has been out of town, told the AP in a telephone interview, adding he had no intention of calling the agent but would “let him waste his time trying to track me down.” “I don’t think there’s any confusion,” he said, adding he intends to rank Democrat Mary Peltola first on his ballot, followed by Dan J. Sullivan. “Everybody knows who the incumbent is.” Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage the federal investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.” The developments come just days before Tuesday’s ranked choice general election in a potentially pivotal race in which Peltola, a former congresswoman, is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. At a campaign rally in Anchorage on Friday, Peltola again denied any involvement in any plan to place candidates on the ballot to detract from the incumbent senator. She said she was “deeply offended” by the allegations, which she called “garbage” and part of a “smear campaign” to suppress turnout on the eve of the election. “I know I can beat Dan Sullivan. I do not need any help winning this race,” she told a small group of campaign volunteers at an Anchorage aviation museum. ___ Mustian reported from New York. Associated Press reporter Becky Bohrer contributed reporting from Juneau, Alaska. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/fbi-visits-dan-j-sullivan-041854344.html

articles.title: Trump's canceled rallies now 'back on' in potential panic move: report
articles.description: President Donald Trump revived campaign rallies in Kansas and Iowa less than a day after canceling them, days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. “Rallies are BACK ON!” read a statement that Fox News White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich posted on X Friday morning, citing a source familiar with the plans. The Republican National Committee had called off both events Thursday, saying that “with Republicans in a strong position in Kansas and Iowa, previously planned in-person rallies in those states will no longer take place as scheduled,” Newsweek reported. Republicans claimed they had called off the rallies because they saw themselves in a strong position in both states, but by Friday morning both were back on. The new statement framed the reversal as a scheduling matter. “President Trump loves his supporters, and in addition to nearly 20 tele-rallies, he will hold back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday,” the statement said. A White House official and a Republican official also confirmed the Sunday plans to CNN. The committee’s announcement Thursday had said that rather than appear in Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday, Trump would spend a “72-hour sprint” holding rallies by phone, which it said would let him reach voters nationwide, CBS News reported. “The rallies were rearranged for scheduling purposes to accommodate dozens of additional tele-rallies that were recently added to the President’s schedule,” Friday’s statement said. On Thursday, the tele-rallies were the reason for the cancellation. On Friday, the rallies were rearranged to make room for those same tele-rallies. Trump said Thursday that the Kansas race didn't need him, and he rejected a suggestion that his health caused the cancellation. “I’m not going to Kansas because he’s doing very well,” Trump said of Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS), according to Newsweek. But new polling showed Marshall trailing Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor, in a state Trump carried by 16 percentage points in 2024, Newsweek reported. The outlet said the canceled rally would have been Trump’s second in Kansas for Marshall this month. “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump said after a reporter asked whether he had canceled the trip because of his health, CBS News reported. “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day,” Trump said in a hoarse voice Monday. He held 25 rallies in October, short of his goal of more than 30. Public polls suggest his visits have not had their intended effect, with Democrats unexpectedly competitive in Iowa, Kansas and other states. Vice President JD Vance also canceled a Friday press conference in Minnesota, CNBC reported. Republicans in Kansas and Iowa were split over whether they wanted Trump to come. Some top Republican operatives in both states quietly expressed relief at the canceled rallies.

articles.title: What to know about the causes of Spain's latest deadly train crash
articles.description: Spain's second major train collision this year has sparked debate over whether human error or rail network failures are to blame. The transport minister has blamed a traffic controller's poor judgment for Wednesday's crash in Toledo province, which killed 69 people. However, railway unions argue that deteriorating working conditions and failing safety systems are the real issues. A judge and a special government commission are investigating. The collision occurred after a communication system malfunction forced human controllers to manage train safety. Unions say the system, which is being phased out, has failed repeatedly. The crash has raised concerns about increased traffic from rail privatization.

articles.title: Brand new law on 5 dog breeds comes into effect this Sunday — criminal offence
The White House Farm massacre phone calls: could a single disputed digit set Jeremy Bamber free?
articles.description: He has been in prison for 41 years for killing five members of his family. But if a phone call was made to the police by Bamber’s father on the night of the murders – as his team believes – one of the UK’s most notorious criminals could be exonerated On 7 August 1985, five people were found dead at White House Farm in Essex, England: 28-year-old Sheila Caffell (known to her family as Bambi); her six-year-old twin sons, Daniel and Nicholas; and her 61-year-old adoptive parents, June and Nevill Bamber. All five had been shot with a rifle. Caffell’s 24-year-old brother, Jeremy Bamber, who was also adopted, had called to alert Essex police to a disturbance inside the farmhouse – he said his father had called to tell him – and had been outside with the police for four hours before the bodies were discovered. Caffell, who had recently been hospitalised with schizoaffective disorder and is said to have feared her children were going to be taken into foster care, was found with the rifle lying on her chest, pointing towards her neck. There were two gunshot wounds to her neck and chin and a bloodied Bible by her side. The case was initially thought to be open and shut, a tragic murder-suicide committed by Caffell. But a month later, Bamber was arrested after relatives went to the police to voice their suspicions about him; his former girlfriend Julie Mugford then told police he had made a confession to her. The relatives went on to inherit from Nevill and June Bamber’s considerable estate after Bamber’s convictions. It was later discovered that Mugford had agreed to sell the story of their relationship to the News of the World for £25,000 if Bamber was convicted. Essex police and crown prosecutors had also agreed to drop charges against her for burglary, chequebook fraud and selling cannabis, because “prosecuting her could jeopardise her availability or credibility as a key witness” against Bamber.
